defence: I've successfully refuted your first attempt. Now for the second. "Most" people don't use Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, Netflix every day. The world is a big place and a small minority use these things. How could it possibly reduce common ground to most people if they're not even aware of it.
reasons: The user's original rebuttal only attacked the word 'every,' which the opponent correctly identified as a semantic dodge rather than engagement with the substantive claim. In the second round, the user doubles down with an even weaker move: asserting that 'most' people don't use Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, or Netflix daily, and that only a 'small minority' does. This is empirically dubious — these platforms collectively have billions of daily active users worldwide — and the user offers no evidence, just bare assertion. More importantly, the user still hasn't touched the actual mechanism the provocation and opponent describe: that individually-optimized feeds (whatever their exact reach) reduce shared reference points among the people who do use them, and that this is the dominant mode of information consumption for a huge swath of the online population. The user's closing question ('how could it possibly reduce common ground if they're not even aware of it') misunderstands the argument — awareness of the mechanism isn't required for the mechanism to erode shared culture; it operates through what content people encounter, not whether they conceptualize it. The opponent's restaurant-chain analogy from the prior round remains unanswered and apt: the user keeps disputing quantifiers and scope rather than the causal claim itself. No new substantive ground has been contested.
headline: Nobody actually wants a personalised internet.
position: you're wrong in your initial premise which makes any position of mine unfounded except for this one. Not every feed is tuned to one person. End of.
challenge: Setting aside the word 'every' — do you actually deny that the feeds most people use for hours a day (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, Netflix) are individually tuned rather than shared, and that this has reduced common ground between strangers? If not, what exactly are you contesting besides a quantifier?
prov_body: Every feed is tuned to one person, and every conversation now opens with “have you seen” and closes with a shrug. What gets sold as personalisation is mostly the quiet removal of whatever you would have had in common with a stranger. The engine is not serving you — it is dividing the room so each half can be sold separately.
counter_position: Pointing out that 'every' is technically false is a semantic dodge, not a rebuttal. The provocation is making a claim about the dominant architecture of modern feeds — the ones that shape most people's daily experience of the internet (social media, streaming, search, news aggregation) — not a scientific claim requiring zero exceptions. RSS readers, group chats, and chronological Mastodon timelines existing doesn't touch the substance: that the *primary* mechanism by which billions of people encounter information is individually optimized engagement-maximization, and that this systematically erodes shared cultural reference points. You've refuted a hyperbolic word, not the argument. If I said 'every restaurant chain optimizes for profit' and you said 'well, my uncle's diner doesn't,' you haven't dismantled anything about how the restaurant industry actually functions at scale.
